newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel business leader warns of possible recession.
newsitem.headline: Israel business leader warns of possible recession.

text.p: Manufacturers Association President Dan Propper on Sunday attacked the Israeli government's 1997 inflation target of seven to 10 percent, saying it could help push the economy into a recession.
"Seven percent is a wild dream, and if the Bank of Israel acts in the direction of seven percent it will bring an even worse slowdown," he said at a news conference.

Propper, who has sharply criticised the central bank's monetary policy, said the target was too wide to serve as a marker. The Treasury would use the upper limit as its goal and the Bank of Israel the lower limit, he said.

Propper said inflation could not realistically fall below nine to 9.5 percent next year. Most of Israel's inflation, he said, was due to monopolies and other structural problems that could not be addressed by monetary policy alone.
He said that the slowdown was approaching the proportions of a recession, especially if aggregate growth slowed in 1997 to the point that per capita growth was nil or even negative.
The Manufacturers Association, Israel's main business lobby, did not offer any projections for growth next year. The Treasury is forecasting a four percent increase in gross domestic product.

Propper said he was most concerned about the slowdown in export growth this year to an estimated seven to 7.5 percent from 11-15 percent in the previous four years. He noted that exports had been the engine of growth in previous years.
But, he said, this year's export growth came almost entirely from electronics and from the increase used of imported components, which lowered the domestic value added.

"The electronics industry has retained its profitability because of the uniqueness of its products," he said. "The problem is that in the other sectors, profitability has fallen and in many cases approaches nil."
Propper said: "If the current policies continue, I don't see continued growth in the electronics sector."

He said the solution was for the government to fulfil its commitment to cutting the budget by seven billion shekels next year and for the central bank to lower the base interest rate two to three percentage points from the current 15.2 percent.
If the government failed, he said, the only solution was for it to make an administrative devaluation by about eight percent.
